lessons.title: Why Malaysia has two sets of rules at once
lessons.summary: Equity is a second body of rules that grew up alongside the common law and can override it. Malaysia received it by statute, on a fixed date, and only so far as local circumstances allow.

sections.keypoint: Two people can both be right about the same land, because two different systems are answering.
sections.h: Two right answers, and neither is wrong

body.text: Encik Rahim holds the title to a shophouse in Ipoh. His name is on the register. His sister Aminah paid for it, and everyone in the family knew the arrangement: he would hold it, she would own it.
Ask who owns the shophouse and you get two answers. The register says Rahim. The family arrangement says Aminah. Both answers are correct. They come from different systems.
The first is the common law answer. It looks at the title and stops. The second is the equitable answer. It asks what the arrangement was, and holds Rahim to it.
This is not a gap in the law. It is the shape of the law. Two bodies of rules run at the same time, and where they collide, equity wins.

sections.keypoint: Equity began as an appeal to the King when the ordinary courts gave a hard answer.
sections.h: Where the second system came from

body.text: The common law courts of England were rigid on purpose. A claim had to fit a recognised form. If it did not fit, there was no remedy, however unfair that was.
People who lost that way petitioned the King. Those petitions went to the Chancellor. Over centuries the Chancellor's answers hardened into rules of their own, and that body of rules is equity.
So equity did not start as a rival system. It started as a complaint about the first one. That origin still shows: equity acts on the conscience of a particular person, not on the world at large.
The common law asks whether Rahim holds the title. He does. Equity asks a different question — whether it would be right for him to keep it for himself. It would not.

sections.keypoint: Section 3 of the Civil Law Act 1956 imports English equity, but frozen at a date.
sections.h: How it reached Malaysia, and when it stopped

body.text: Malaysia did not grow equity. It received it, by statute.

Section 3 of the Civil Law Act 1956 applies the common law of England and the rules of equity as administered in England on a fixed date. For the States of Malaya that date is 7 April 1956. Sabah and Sarawak have their own earlier dates.
Two things follow, and both matter. English decisions after the cut-off date are not automatically part of Malaysian law. And the reception is qualified.
The qualification is that the received rules apply only so far as local circumstances permit, and subject to any local written law. A rule that does not fit here does not arrive here.
It is easy to read a recent English judgment and assume it states Malaysian law. Sometimes a Malaysian court adopts it. That is a choice the court makes, not something section 3 did for it.

sections.keypoint: Equity works on people, and only for those who come to it with clean hands.
sections.h: What equity will not do for you

body.text: Equity is not sympathy. It has conditions, and they are strict.

items: **It acts on the person.** An equitable order tells a named person what to do. It does not rewrite the register by itself.
**It will not help the unclean.** A claimant who behaved badly in the same matter can be refused, however good the claim looks.
**It will not help the slow.** Sit on a right for years and equity may treat it as abandoned.
**It follows the law.** Where a statute is clear, equity does not overrule it.

body.prompt: Aminah waits eleven years, then asks a court to make Rahim transfer the shophouse. What is the first thing the other side will say?
body.reveal: That she was too slow. Delay is one of the standard answers to an equitable claim, and it is an answer about her conduct rather than about who paid.

quiz.q: Under section 3 of the Civil Law Act 1956, what happened to English equity?
options: It was applied in full and continues to update automatically
It was rejected in favour of a Malaysian code
It applies only in Sabah and Sarawak
It was applied as it stood at a fixed date, subject to local circumstances
quiz.why: Section 3 receives the rules as administered in England at a stated date, and only so far as local circumstances and local written law permit.

quiz.q: Rahim holds the registered title; Aminah paid and the family agreed she would own it. Which is true?
options: Both answers are correct, because two systems are answering different questions
Only Rahim has any claim, because the register is conclusive
Only Aminah has any claim, because she paid
Neither has a claim until a court decides
quiz.why: The common law looks at the title; equity asks whether it would be right to keep the benefit. Both are correct within their own system.

quiz.q: Why is it wrong to assume a 2019 English judgment states Malaysian law?
options: English judgments never apply in Malaysia
It postdates the reception date, so a Malaysian court must choose to adopt it
Only Federal Court decisions apply here
Equity was never received in Malaysia
quiz.why: Section 3 fixes the reception at a date. Later English decisions may be persuasive, but adopting one is a decision the Malaysian court makes.

lessons.source: Civil Law Act 1956, s 3, for the reception and its date. The account of equity's origins is standard legal history and is not tied to any single authority.
lessons.verify: Read section 3 of the Civil Law Act 1956 itself, and check the dates for Sabah and Sarawak against the section rather than against this page.

reading.where: section 3 — the reception provision, including its cut-off date. One section carries the whole argument of this lesson

lessons.title: When an arrangement is actually a trust
lessons.summary: A trust splits ownership in two: one person holds, another benefits. Three things must be certain before a court will find one, and a promise to be generous is not among them.

sections.keypoint: A trust separates the person who holds a thing from the person it is really for.

body.text: Puan Siti is dying. She has RM80,000 and a son who is nine. She does not want the money handed to a child, so she gives it to her brother and tells him to use it for the boy's schooling.
The brother now holds the money. He cannot spend it on himself. He holds it for the boy, and a court will make him do it.
That is a trust. Three people have roles. Siti set it up, the brother holds, the boy benefits.

In a trust, legal ownership and beneficial ownership are held by different people. The trustee holds the property. The beneficiary is entitled to the benefit of it. The trustee's duties are owed to the beneficiary and are enforceable by them.
body.source: General principle of trusts law as received under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3.

sections.keypoint: Three things must be certain: the intention, the property, and who benefits.
sections.h: The three things that must be certain

body.text: Not every generous arrangement is a trust. Courts ask three questions, and all three must be answered.

body.caption: The three certainties, and what fails without each
rows: Did the giver mean to impose a duty, or only express a hope?
No trust. The recipient keeps the property outright.
Is it clear which property is held, and what share each beneficiary takes?
No trust. A court cannot administer what it cannot identify.
Is it clear who the beneficiaries are?
No trust. There is nobody with standing to enforce it.
body.alt: Three certainties in a table. Intention: did the giver impose a duty or only express a hope — without it the recipient keeps the property outright. Subject matter: is the property and each share identified — without it a court cannot administer the trust. Objects: is it clear who benefits — without it nobody can enforce.

body.text: Notice that each failure has a different consequence. That is worth holding on to. The three certainties are not one test with three parts.

sections.keypoint: Hoping someone will be generous is not the same as ordering them to be.

body.text: The first certainty causes the most trouble, because people do not write like lawyers when they are dying.

Two wordings. "I leave my house to my brother, trusting he will look after my daughter." And: "I leave my house to my brother to hold for my daughter until she is 21." The first expresses a hope. The second imposes a duty.
The court looks at what the words did, not at which words were used. There is no magic in the word trust, and a trust can exist without it.
The test is whether a duty was imposed on the holder. If the holder could honestly keep the property and breach nothing, there is no trust.
This cuts both ways. A document that says trust everywhere may still fail, if reading it shows the holder was left free to do as they liked.

sections.keypoint: Some trusts are imposed by law, whatever the parties intended.

body.text: So far the trusts have been deliberate. Someone meant to create one. Two other kinds arise without that.

items: **A resulting trust** sends the benefit back. Aminah pays for the shophouse and Rahim takes the title. Unless a gift was intended, equity treats him as holding it for her.
**A constructive trust** is imposed by law on a person whose conscience is affected — most obviously someone who takes property knowing it was meant for another.

body.text: Both are responses, not arrangements. Nobody signs anything. The court finds the trust because of what happened.

body.prompt: Rahim sells the shophouse to a buyer who knows about the family arrangement. Does the buyer take it free of Aminah's interest?
body.reveal: Knowledge is the whole question. A buyer who knows of the arrangement may find their own conscience affected — which is how equity reaches a person who was never party to the original deal.

quiz.q: A will reads: "to my brother, trusting he will look after my daughter". What is the likely result?
options: A valid trust, because the word trusting was used
A valid trust, because a daughter is named
No trust, because the words express a hope rather than a duty
No trust, because a will cannot create one
quiz.why: Certainty of intention asks whether a duty was imposed. Words of hope leave the holder free, and there is no magic in the word trust.

quiz.q: A trust says the trustee holds "some of my shares" for a named nephew. Which certainty fails?
options: Intention
Subject matter
Objects
None — it is valid
quiz.why: The beneficiary is identified and a duty is clearly imposed, but nobody can say which shares are held. A court cannot administer property it cannot identify.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a resulting and a constructive trust?
options: A resulting trust sends the benefit back to the provider; a constructive trust is imposed because a conscience is affected
A resulting trust is written down; a constructive trust is oral
A resulting trust applies to land only; a constructive trust to money only
There is no difference in Malaysian law
quiz.why: Both arise by operation of law rather than by arrangement, but they answer different questions — where the benefit should return, and whose conscience is affected.

quiz.q: Why does certainty of objects matter?
options: Because trustees must be paid
Because without an identifiable beneficiary there is nobody who can enforce the trustee's duties
Because a trust must be registered
Because the settlor must be alive
quiz.why: A trustee's duties are owed to the beneficiaries. With no identifiable beneficiary, the duty has nobody to enforce it and the court cannot supervise it.

lessons.source: The three certainties and the two non-express trusts are standard trusts doctrine, received in Malaysia under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3.
lessons.verify: This lesson deliberately states no case citations. Check each proposition against a Malaysian trusts text before relying on it, and note that reception under section 3 is subject to local circumstances.

reading.where: section 3 again, this time as the authority for trusts doctrine applying here at all
